changes.before: Minnesota has no reliable current count of Amharic speakers. The Census Bureau estimated 9,490 Amharic speakers age 5 and older in Minnesota for 2009-2013 (give or take 1,009), seventh among states; since then its standard tables group Amharic with Somali and other Afro-Asiatic languages. Minnesota schools reported 2,379 students with Amharic as their primary home language in 2024-25, 948 of them English learners. MPR reported in 2005 that the State Demographer's office estimated about 7,500 Ethiopian immigrants in the state, and that immigrant groups said the number was about double. An undated project request to the Minnesota House estimates 45,000 to 50,000 people in and around the Twin Cities who identify as Ethiopian or Ethiopian American, but that is a figure from a funding request, and it counts ethnicity and not language. Not every Ethiopian speaks Amharic as a first language, and Oromo, Tigrinya and Anywaa speakers have their own organizations. Worthington's daily newspaper reported on an Ethiopian Orthodox congregation there in 2020 and 2022, under the names Menbere Tsehay Saint Mary and Tsadakane Mariam, and we could not confirm its current address or whether these are one congregation. The list below is starting points for learning. It is not complete, and listing here says nothing about who a person trusts.
changes.reason: Separate language estimates, ethnicity estimates, local verification limits and use of the directory so readers do not conflate their evidence.
changes.after:
Minnesota has no reliable current count of Amharic speakers. The Census Bureau estimated 9,490 Amharic speakers age 5 and older in Minnesota for 2009-2013 (give or take 1,009), seventh among states; since then its standard tables group Amharic with Somali and other Afro-Asiatic languages. Minnesota schools reported 2,379 students with Amharic as their primary home language in 2024-25, 948 of them English learners. MPR reported in 2005 that the State Demographer's office estimated about 7,500 Ethiopian immigrants in the state, and that immigrant groups said the number was about double.

An undated project request to the Minnesota House estimates 45,000 to 50,000 people in and around the Twin Cities who identify as Ethiopian or Ethiopian American, but that is a figure from a funding request, and it counts ethnicity and not language. Not every Ethiopian speaks Amharic as a first language, and Oromo, Tigrinya and Anywaa speakers have their own organizations.

Worthington's daily newspaper reported on an Ethiopian Orthodox congregation there in 2020 and 2022, under the names Menbere Tsehay Saint Mary and Tsadakane Mariam, and we could not confirm its current address or whether these are one congregation.

The list below offers starting points for learning. It is not complete, and listing here says nothing about who a person trusts.

changes.before: Johnnie Lacy was born in 1937 and spent her childhood in Arkansas and Louisiana during segregation; in 1947, when she was 10, her family moved to California, where she lived in McCloud. She attended Chico State from 1954 to 1956 and was studying toward nursing when she contracted polio in 1956, at 19. From 1958 to 1960 she majored in speech therapy at San Francisco State, a campus that was not accessible; the department head tried to block her enrollment, and she was not allowed to take part in graduation.
